title: Mortgage arrears in Ontario approaching levels last seen in 2008 financial crisis
html:
A growing number of homeowners in Ontario are finding themselves unable to pay their mortgages due to high mortgage balances and rising interest rates, even as delinquency rates ease in much of the rest of the country.

A recent report from TD Bank economist Maria Solovieva found the rate of homeowners in arrears has nearly tripled from prepandemic norms of 0.12 per cent to 0.34 per cent in Ontario. That equates to roughly one in every 300 households falling behind on mortgage payments for three or more months.

The rate is approaching levels not seen since the 2008 financial crisis, when mortgage arrears in Ontario reached a peak of 0.43 per cent.

Economists and credit experts say the number of households in the province falling behind on their mortgages is expected to increase through 2027, with more interest rate increases likely leading to more banks being forced to sell properties owned by borrowers who have fallen far behind on payments.

They say Ontario is faring much worse than the rest of the country because mortgage balances in the province are so large, which has left many consumers with little wiggle room to cope with increases in interest rates since the pandemic.

Although mortgage arrears have also been rising quickly in British Columbia, the pace of increase there has slowed, while Ontario’s has not, the TD report noted.

The Ontario market is also seeing a larger housing market downturn, particularly in small condos that were generally purchased by investors.

Meanwhile, Ms. Solovieva said in cities such as Hamilton and Oshawa, higher rates of unemployment in the manufacturing sector tied to the U.S. trade war are compounding the problem. She cited Statistics Canada figures from October that found 35 per cent of people living in households in Oshawa, Windsor and Hamilton reported difficulties meeting their financial needs, the highest level among Canada’s largest cities.

“Ontario is one of the weakest economies in Canada currently with pressure coming from U.S. tariffs, and it is seeing a higher unemployment rate,” Ms. Solovieva said.

“There is a combination of income shock and payment shock from higher interest rates.”

She expects delinquencies will continue to increase until the second quarter of 2027, when TD Bank is forecasting the economy and employment rates will begin to improve.

Doug Hoyes, a licensed insolvency trustee and co-founder of Hoyes, Michalos and Associates in Toronto, said he expects the housing market will continue to feel the impact of mortgage arrears for much longer.

He is noticing a higher number of clients who are are having a lender force what’s known as a power-of-sale, in which a mortgage provider forces a sale of the borrower’s property to recover funds. Realtors have said these kinds of sales are becoming increasingly common in the Toronto-area market.

Mr. Hoyes said lenders often wait months or even a year to force a sale, because a sale in the current housing market downturn often fetches prices significantly lower than the value at which the property was appraised when the mortgage was issued.

Among Ontario’s struggling borrowers are also scores of real estate investors who purchased preconstruction condos and are finding themselves unable to secure a mortgage because property values have dropped below the price they agreed to pay, Mr. Hoyes said. In these scenarios, condo developers are generally the ones who eventually have to try and sell those units, rather than the banks.

Rebecca Oakes, vice-president of advanced analytics at credit reporting agency Equifax Canada, said rising interest rates could delay a recovery in mortgage arrears rates.

Fixed mortgage rates have increased in recent months, driven by bond yields that are rising due to investor concerns about inflation and fiscal policy in the U.S.

Growing concerns about inflation also prompted the Bank of Canada to raise its key interest rate – by a quarter of a percentage point – for the first time in three years in October. The central bank’s rate influences variable mortgage rates, which tend to move in tandem with it. Financial markets expect three more hikes in 2027, and each hike will increase borrowing costs for variable-mortgage holders.

“Every quarter-point increase starts to put added financial pressure on homeowners,” Ms. Oakes said.

Ms. Solovieva added that Canada’s job market will also have a significant impact on whether mortgage arrears rates will improve. She said a prolonging of the trade war could delay a recovery for Canadian household balance sheets.

“If we have more pressure coming from [the trade war] and it impacts employment and there are layoffs, then we could see unemployment rates rising and more deterioration.”
summary: Rate of homeowners in arrears nearly tripled from prepandemic norms
